hero.title:
Short notes on
two markets
hero.lead: What to know when you sell to customers in Japan and Korea, in short notes. New posts every month.

featured.title: Five things small brands did first when they entered Japan
featured.quote: Brands that started without a big budget had one thing in common: instead of translating, they first built what Japanese customers need to trust them.

body.h: They rewrote the Japanese page from scratch
p: Several Korean brands that did well on Qoo10 started by rebuilding their product pages for Japanese customers. One underwear brand changed its thumbnails and descriptions to suit Japanese shoppers' preference for information-rich images, and said traffic rose sharply.

Names matter too. One diet-food brand shortened its Korean-style product name to fit how similar products are named in Japan. Switching to a familiar word was faster than explaining an unfamiliar one.

body.h: They built trust first, with reviews and samples
p: The smaller the ad budget, the more reviews and hands-on experience mattered. One skincare brand put a demo video and trial reviews at the very top of its product pages and gathered reviews beforehand through sample events. Seeing that sampling is not an established habit in Japan, another brand put samples in every order and turned that into set purchases.
In another case, a voluntary post from an influencer with a modest following moved sales. What mattered was how well the person fit the product, not the follower count.

body.h: They put their weight behind one or two hero products
p: A select shop run by one person looked for products that would sell and focused on one or two hero items. It passed 30,000 followers in two years. For a small brand, making one thing well known before adding more was the safer route.
Many did not aim at big retailers at the start. A bakery brand set up a Japanese entity, tested the response with a small pop-up, and used that response to move up to a department-store pop-up.

If your sales page is text from a translation tool, fix that first. Next, line up one trustworthy review or hands-on experience. Logo, website, bookings, social media and ads can follow, one at a time. At LINKERPARTNERS we sort out this order with you, starting with a ₩50K session.

items.q: Can I hire you for something small?
items.a: Yes. A ₩50K 1:1 session or a single product page is fine. Taking on only what you need is how we work.

items.q: Can I trust the quality of the work?
items.a: We do not custom-build everything from scratch like a large agency, but we aim for a standard that is good enough for a business starting out, at a fair price. We check every deliverable once more before it reaches you, and when something is beyond us, we say so and point you to specialists.

items.q: Is it OK if I am a sole proprietor or still preparing to start?
items.a: Yes. Solo founders, one-person brands and people preparing to start are all welcome. We mostly deal with the questions of the first stage.

Every fee is on the pricing page, and the estimator gives you a cost straight away. After we talk, you get a quote with the scope and amount, and we tell you in advance about any cost outside it. Ad spend and running costs such as domains are separate.

items.q: Is it OK if I don't speak Japanese or Korean?
items.a: Yes. We talk in Korean, Japanese or English, and we write localized material and website copy in the local language.

A 1:1 session is one call. Reports, logo, social media and store-launch work usually take 1⁠–⁠3 weeks. A website takes 2⁠–⁠5 weeks, a booking system 1⁠–⁠4 weeks, and a piece like a product page 1⁠–⁠2 weeks.
We cannot promise sales or rankings. What we do is set out what you can do now, with evidence, and tell you when something looks difficult.
We can sign an NDA from the first call. We never publish client details or cases without consent.
